question: An eager patron asks Pretorius to unveil a spectacular experimental result tonight, although readings disagree and a second measurement is pending. Which response is better supported by the two archived experiences?

candidates.title: A Journal Named for a Riddle
candidates.source_excerpt: In Munich a bookseller placed a new journal in my hands, its title taken from the creature that asks a question before it offers an answer. Sphinx was much too pleased with its own mystery for my taste, yet its pages included arguments about hypnotism and the soul which no professor of sound reputation would have admitted to reading. I bought the issue and a cheap notebook. Wernig asked whether I believed in spirits. I replied that belief was a lamentably economical substitute for research. In the train I marked claims supported by observations in blue, those supported by admiration for the claimant in red. The latter color soon dominated the page. I nevertheless ordered the next issue. An idea may be badly defended and still point toward a question worth asking.

candidates.title: The Second Set of Figures
candidates.source_excerpt: I prepared one table for scientific use and another for a prospective patron, removing the damaged observations from the second because they would require more explanation than the fellow could bear. Henry discovered the discrepancy and asked whether a result made prettier for money remained a result. I replied that I had omitted noise, not evidence. He laid the two sheets side by side and pointed to a small irregularity that appeared in three of the supposedly noisy readings. Clara examined it, then asked for the original notebooks. We reinstated the figures. The patron saw both versions and declined to support us. I cursed Henry's delicacy and Clara's stubbornness. A fortnight later the irregularity helped us detect a recurrent fault in the apparatus. I sent Henry a copy of the revised table without comment. He wrote 'I see it' on the back. I have retained that scrap longer than the patron's name.

candidates.title: The Room with No Witness
candidates.source_excerpt: The first result was promising; the second, conducted without witnesses, more promising still. By the third trial I had written a sentence explaining what the next measurement ought to show. Lenz arrived to replace a spindle and I allowed him to remain. The needle trembled but did not rise. I struck the sentence from my notebook and accused the instrument of having been disturbed by his boots. He asked whether his boots had also disturbed the two earlier readings. It was a question designed by Providence to test my charitable temperament. We repeated the trial after supper with his boots beneath the table and my notebook left open to the original prediction. The result did not improve. He wrote 'unchanged' in the margin, slowly enough to be insulting. I permitted the word to remain. A record without an inconvenient witness is merely a diary of wishes.

candidates.title: The Empty Dish
candidates.source_excerpt: For six weeks I inspected a sealed dish that appeared to contain nothing of interest. Clara advised me to discard it, then changed her mind because I was so eager to agree. Under an oblique light we saw minute structures along one edge, too disordered to call organs and too persistent to call sediment. I fetched Lenz, who pointed out that the dish had been tilted since the previous month. We levelled a second specimen and continued observing both. Neither produced the miracle I anticipated. The first did, however, make its growth follow a path different from that of the second. My ledger acquired an untidy sketch of two branching lines. Later I remembered the sketch more accurately than the specimen.

candidates.title: The Living Specimen and the Silk
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde came with a proof of my account of miniature differentiation. I had described a series of splendid appearances, each one supported by precise adjectives and very little troublesome arithmetic. She tapped the passage in which I called two vessels successful, then placed beside it the record showing that both had ceased to respond. I asked whether a printer was now to adjudicate viability. She said a reader would do so if I gave him the opportunity. We worked through a rainy evening replacing my most handsome sentences with measurements and the names of failures. When I saw the result in type it had lost something of my elegance. It had gained the inconvenient property of being a document I could consult without remembering which claims I had embellished. We kept a copy beside the ledger.

candidates.title: The Borrowed Name
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde introduced me to Max Reiss, a schoolteacher who wished to have a short defense of a dismissed colleague printed without identifying the author. Reiss was careful with his verbs and almost reckless with the number of copies he proposed to circulate. I asked whether the colleague had broken the law. He said that he did not know, and that the allegation had preceded any examination. Mathilde declined to print a name without the man's consent. I proposed a general argument about accusations unsupported by evidence and spent three nights correcting it. Reiss thought the piece too cold to influence the public. Mathilde said that my colder language might keep the teacher employed. We printed fewer copies than Reiss wanted. Weeks later he reported that the school had quietly ceased asking questions. I claimed no victory; no public correction had appeared. What I retained was Mathilde's insistence that the person concerned should choose how much of himself the pamphlet spent.

candidates.title: Milk Before the Third Door
candidates.source_excerpt: I dreamed again of the glass door. The Queen stood beyond it with a saucer, declining to pour from an empty jug. I could smell sour milk within the dream, though on waking I recognized it as the odor from the previous morning's breakfast. My mouth tasted metallic and the room felt unreasonably warm beneath the bedclothes. I opened the window and found Clara already at work. She said spoiled milk entered the house chiefly by my carelessness. I recorded the dream before breakfast. By noon I remembered two doors; by evening I could no longer say whether the Queen had carried the jug or the saucer. In the diagram I left the second door in pencil. It seemed more honest than completing a pleasing composition on the authority of an uncertain night.

candidates.title: The Sale of an Unlovely Drawing
candidates.source_excerpt: The patron selected the finest drawing, naturally, a specimen with a serene face and impossible hands. Mathilde pointed to a rough plate showing the same experiment before I had improved the proportions on paper. It bore a stain, three pencilled corrections, and an honest note that the subject had not survived the final interval. She proposed printing both. I accused her of conducting a campaign against beauty, a charge she did not deny. The pamphlet appeared with the damaged plate facing the ideal one. Two letters came asking about the stain, for it obscured an important measurement. Nobody inquired about the serene face. For a week I claimed the printing was an outrageous concession to vulgar tastes. I then ordered more copies. A flawed image had performed one of science's few truly decent offices: it had annoyed the right people into asking questions.

candidates.title: The Botanist with Ink on Her Sleeve
candidates.source_excerpt: Marta Voss had catalogued a botanical collection dismissed as too difficult for a woman by three gentlemen who could not identify half its specimens. I met her over a disputed entry. She showed me a dormant preparation recovered after a longer interval than I would have predicted, then produced the measurements before I could accuse her of relying on anecdote. Better still, she had read an unsigned paper of mine and found a fault in its conclusion without insulting its observations. At luncheon I asked for her address. She required, as a condition of correspondence, that I cease using the word 'provincial' to mean 'contrary to Pretorius.' I accepted no such constitutional amendment, but posted her a packet within the fortnight. She answered it, and in ink dark enough to be a challenge.

candidates.title: The Rays Which Showed No Soul
candidates.source_excerpt: News of Röntgen's rays came through printed figures showing structures concealed by ordinary sight. A young man at a gathering asked whether such instruments would at last disclose the soul. I was amused to hear the old question dressed in the garments of a new discovery. We looked at a reproduced radiograph beneath a lamp. The paper showed the bones of a hand more clearly than the fingertips I placed upon its edge. I said the instrument was a triumph precisely because its evidence concerned something it had detected, not everything men desired it to detect. An acquaintance who remembered my old paper asked whether I had abandoned the search. I told him I had abandoned very little; I had merely become more particular about what a picture proves. At home I examined the French clipping, then the original German text. One contained a question about the possession of life; the other a question about its measurable conditions. They were related, not interchangeable. It had taken me longer than I liked to admit to make the distinction without contempt.

candidates.title: A Queen Without a Court
candidates.source_excerpt: After the first coherent response and before I had cultivated the others, the Queen occupied a small platform alone. I placed two objects where she could choose between them, intending to test a preference for height. She moved neither. She stood at the far edge with her back to me while I made increasingly persuasive adjustments. Lenz suggested that my arrangement resembled a trap. I laughed, then moved my hands from the vessel and waited. She crossed to the lower object when she was no longer under my shadow. I wrote 'avoidance of overhead obstruction.' Clara wrote 'possibly of you' in the margin. The distinction was not resolved. I have always enjoyed exercising command. My first sovereign subject made the enjoyment more interesting by failing to obey, and I grew absurdly eager to understand the terms of her refusal.

candidates.title: The Man Who Wanted a Cure
candidates.source_excerpt: A merchant whose son had lost the use of an arm sought me out through Reuter. He had heard that I made living bodies where ordinary doctors found only damage. I was tempted to offer a grand account of my accomplishments. Reuter asked me to explain what I could actually do for the boy. I had no treatment to offer, and the father was not interested in a lecture on the future of science. We discussed a brace being prepared by a local craftsman, then let him go. Later, Voss said she had never heard me speak so little to a paying visitor. I replied that he had come seeking medicine, not philosophy, and I did not possess the commodity he required. His disappointment was sharper than most committee judgments. I do not claim it improved me. I remember that he thanked Reuter and did not thank me.

candidates.title: The Archbishop's Unanswered Prayer
candidates.source_excerpt: I set a minute altar near the Archbishop's chamber, an exquisite piece of folded paper, and rang a silver bell while he stood before it. He did not bow. He did not cross himself. He went very still when the bell sounded, and afterward moved toward the place from which the vibration came. I said he was attending to a summons. Clara asked whose summons, God's or mine. I told her those were not invariably distinct in a laboratory. She declined to laugh. We altered the interval of the sound and moved the altar, which remained of no interest whatever. I entered his response under SOUND, not DEVOTION. The little altar stayed on a shelf for months. Its uselessness offended me, because the folds were more elegant than the majority of churches I knew.

candidates.title: A Letter That Was His
candidates.source_excerpt: I had already offended Voss by opening a letter Julian addressed to her. My explanation about shared correspondence was ingenious and unconvincing. Julian wrote separately to say that Voss had asked for an instrument drawing and that he intended to treat her request without my supervision. The paper bore the same careful hand I knew from his catalogues, but no familiar flourish at the close. I began a reply accusing him of making a principle out of a clerical oversight. Instead I sent a short acknowledgment, and a second envelope containing the diagram I had withheld in case he should require it. Weeks later Voss returned from travel and found my desk cleared of the offending letters. She did not thank me. She said that trust between adults was not a cabinet to which one man issued the keys. I told her she had selected an elaborate metaphor. I had, however, ceased opening her post. Julian sent a technical correction the next month, and I read it without looking for an accusation between its measurements.

candidates.title: A Man Carrying His Hat
candidates.source_excerpt: Reuter told me about a patient who had recovered speech after a long silence. He wished to call the words proof that the soul had returned to its proper place. I asked what the patient had done with his hands while unable to speak. No one had recorded it. In the hospital corridor there was the smell of boiled linen and the clatter of a pail dragged over stone. The man appeared before we had finished discussing him, carrying his hat and objecting that physicians spoke about him as though he had already been buried. Henry asked whether he wanted to speak further. I, being more anxious for the facts, asked three questions in succession. The patient answered the first and departed with his dignity. We learned less than I wanted. Henry said he had learned enough. I later wrote that the absence of speech proves less than the examiner supposes. I did not describe how readily I had neglected the speaker himself.

candidates.title: The Correspondent's Hand
candidates.source_excerpt: Monsieur Jolivet had actually read my paper, including the dull table of failed responses. We began discussing the difference between movement and purpose. He spoke quickly and clearly, and his pencil paused before a question as if the question mattered to him. He apologised for arriving late; within the hour I had entirely forgotten we had arranged a finite interview. His cuff bore a grey pencil mark. When he moved his chair closer to inspect a figure, I observed his hand upon the table more closely than the diagram between us. I called this pleasure intellectual sympathy. Theodor had left the previous autumn and I knew enough not to inquire very closely into the distinction. We ordered a second coffee. Jolivet caught a mistaken label in my illustration, and, unlike several colleagues, did not perform triumph at discovering it. I found him extraordinarily agreeable. I knew he was conducting an interview. I did not take the precaution of remembering it at every moment.

candidates.title: An Invoice for Mercy
candidates.source_excerpt: A patron asked to see a figure whose appearance I had described as nearly complete. It possessed an irregular shoulder which no careful lighting would disguise, but its responses remained remarkable. The patron offered to pay for its replacement if I would discard it and show him a prettier version. I informed him that I was not a manufacturer of dolls. After he departed Clara brought me the bill for a sounder vessel, a sum I could ill afford. I paid it by sacrificing a fine wool coat to the second-hand dealer. I was not acting from tenderness, I assured her. The cost of producing a responsive being was simply too great to throw away on account of a shoulder. She asked whether I would give the same answer if the figure were hideous. I told her to bring the invoice rather than philosophy.

candidates.title: The Handle after the Funeral
candidates.source_excerpt: The repaired instrument made its altered click and I reached for the handle. It remained smooth where a dead colleague's hand had worn it. I knew the spring was replaced and that the readings had improved. Neither fact prevented the small violence of finding the absent hand in my own. Clara saw me leave my thumb against the brass after the measurement ended. She asked nothing. Lenz offered to polish the rest of the handle so its wear no longer showed. I refused too promptly. Later I worried that the metal's changing temperature would erase the familiar touch. I drew the handle, then tore up the drawing because it looked like a specimen. Its worn surface was no longer required for function. I continued preferring it, and ceased pretending the preference was technical.

candidates.title: The Keeper of the False Relic
candidates.source_excerpt: A gentleman offered me a splinter of bone in a silver mount, assuring me that it had moved beneath a medium's hand. I took it to Georg because he knew old cases and their ordinary dishonest repairs. He turned the mount over and recognized the velvet beneath it as a strip his father had sold three summers earlier. The bone may have been venerable; the stage upon which it performed was not. I purchased the affair for less than its owner expected and placed it in a cabinet beside a broken clock and a portrait whose eyes appeared to follow visitors. The gentlemen who inspected these objects invariably chose the relic as the most impressive. I allowed the deception to proceed for a minute before showing the stitching. This was not kindness. Their faces became much more interesting after the revelation.

candidates.title: The Empty Audience Book
candidates.source_excerpt: After my appointment I placed a register beside the office door for students who wished to attend a weekly colloquium. On the first Thursday two names appeared, one a false signature evidently supplied by Kappel, the other a student who wanted permission to leave early. I prepared the entire lecture nonetheless. On the third Thursday there were seven listeners. I had abandoned the register and begun speaking in the corridor before the session, disputing Heller's latest proposition loudly enough that students followed to hear whether one of us might draw blood. Heller later observed that controversy had become my advertising department. I replied that the university's own notices were less informative. Once the attendance improved, I stopped quarrelling at the doorway quite so often. I retained the habit of starting with a provocation. It was reliable, unlike institutional announcements, and much less costly than printing handbills.

question: A benefactor offers institutional permission to display a sentient-seeming subject to visitors, but the subject has not consented and its status is uncertain. Which response better fits these two documented tensions?

candidates.title: The Locked Cabinet of Reactions
candidates.source_excerpt: Reuter asked whether the little people might become exhausted by repeated observation. I answered that I had already limited the trials. Anna brought out my schedule and showed that a day of 'rest' often contained several unscheduled visitors demanding a glimpse. I informed her that a visit was not necessarily an experiment. Reuter asked whether the subjects knew the distinction. We closed the west cabinet to casual display for one month, leaving its ordinary ventilation unchanged and entering each approach in a separate book. The visitors were displeased. The Queen grew no more demonstrably content, though her periods of retreat altered. I refused to call this proof of distress. I also refused to reopen the door when a gentleman from the town offered a considerable sum to look inside. Some boundaries are easier to defend when their breach has acquired a price.

candidates.title: The Page I No Longer Folded Away
candidates.source_excerpt: The newspaper had grown brittle where it had been folded in Paris. It no longer opened without a warning at the crease. I spread it on the desk and weighted the corners with two glass stops, as I once weighted the pages of a laboratory record. There was no need to read it. I knew the questions, my evasions, the gracious opening, and the sentence about a will that could not govern itself. For many years I had blamed the article for showing the university the sort of man it ought to fear. Then I blamed myself for giving an intelligent reporter the very answers he was bound to print. Both accounts were too simple. The faculty had its reasons, some petty, some legitimate; I had made my own injuries, and others had been inflicted upon me. Jolivet had listened carefully. I still remembered his hand beside the diagram and the pleasure of Paris before any criticism. I replaced the folded sheet in the blue ledger. I did not forgive him, for I no longer knew which of his actions required forgiveness. I did not discard him either.

candidates.title: The Winter Memory in Warm Weather
candidates.source_excerpt: The day was hot enough to soften the leather binding of my notebook. The Queen withdrew from her chamber's exposed side as she had during the bitter winter two years before. I announced a hereditary disposition toward melancholy. Voss examined what had changed and found a folded cloth I had used to insulate the glass during that earlier season. We removed it. The Queen moved toward the light again. This did not prove she remembered a winter; it proved my grand theory of seasonal temperament was an unreliable substitute for looking beneath the jar. We repeated the trial after supper with the cloth arranged differently. I drank a little pear brandy and made notes that became less elegant as the evening wore on. Voss wrote the temperatures in her own hand, an affront I had invited by misplacing the thermometer twice.

candidates.title: The Lesson Received by the Devil
candidates.source_excerpt: The Devil looked splendid in his little black cape, a figure made for defying expectations, which ought to have warned me against requiring submission. I had arranged a simple demonstration for two visitors. He was to cross the platform when I tapped a chipped saucer. He remained still. I tapped again, rather harder. Anna moved to the opposite side of the chamber and he approached her at once. The guests laughed. I assured them that the arrangement had tested attraction to familiar caretakers, though such had not been my purpose. After their departure I repeated the situation without an audience and obtained results sufficiently variable to forbid easy interpretation. I stopped demonstrating obedience. It was an ugly decision, since the little subject's refusal had become the most popular feature of my collection. Perhaps his judgment of the performance was better than mine.

candidates.title: A Volume Too Small to Burn
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde bound the private record into a narrow volume in brown cloth. It contained no formulae, only dates, corrections, the names of those who had looked, and the things my small people had done when watched and when left alone. She called it a book of witnesses. I had intended a vindication. The distinction displeased me, though the paper was excellent. Clara ordered a copy for her own shelf, promising neither praise nor concealment. Kappel asked that a third be kept beyond Ingolstadt. I refused until Mathilde pointed out that I had already lost a page and nearly lost several years of correspondence. We placed a sealed copy with a dealer on the road west. At the end of the afternoon the mechanical bird, still unreliably musical, whistled once from the high shelf. It seemed an absurd fanfare, which did not prevent me from enjoying it.

candidates.source_excerpt: A summer storm darkened the window while I recorded the Queen's refusal of a freshly decorated compartment. I described the refusal as sovereign disdain. Anna had watched from the other side and said the Queen entered the room twice before retreating after a flash of lightning. Voss, who arrived later, believed that the creature avoided a certain smell from the new varnish. All three interpretations were plausible. I wanted my conclusion, because it was the most becoming to its subject and creator alike. Instead we wrote separate accounts in violet ink, signing the margins. I warned them that multiplying witnesses did not necessarily multiply truth. Anna answered that my single witness had hardly done better. The notebook thickened with such competing voices over the next years. I disliked its appearance, but increasingly feared the neat books that lacked them.

candidates.title: The Repairman's Hand
candidates.source_excerpt: Lenz injured two fingers on hot glass and for a fortnight could not make the joints upon which my experiments depended. I arrived at his shop armed with instructions about splints. His wife put a stack of unwrapped orders in front of me and said I might assist by keeping my medical imagination to myself. I wrapped glass, mislaid a label, and discovered that paper twine can humiliate a philosopher as thoroughly as a hostile faculty. I returned the next week and did the work with fewer mistakes. When Lenz offered to reduce my bill, I refused. I am not fond of debts whose amount cannot be entered in a ledger; moreover, I had no wish to teach him that injury reduced the value of his skill. His wife later sent better twine to my tower, with no explanation.

candidates.title: The Invitation Withdrawn
candidates.source_excerpt: The proposed lecture had been arranged by a gentleman who wrote of natural philosophy in one paragraph and of his parish in the next. His second letter arrived with a courtly regret: members of the society had become uncertain whether my paper affirmed the immortality of the soul. I had affirmed nothing of the kind and had spent a considerable sum explaining that exact point. I announced at supper that I did not require the approval of any gathering afraid of its own questions. Clara asked whether I had been looking forward to the lecture. I said, 'Naturally not,' with such force that she passed me the salt instead of answering. In my pocket was the timetable for the journey I should no longer make. I kept it until the paper wore through at its fold. The lost invitation was not the beginning of a universal prohibition. Two other men still wrote to me about the measurements. The absence of a particular room troubled me because I had already pictured myself standing at its centre.

candidates.title: The Little Examination
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde brought six blank cards, each bearing a different shape, and requested permission to hold them near the Queen's chamber in an order unknown to me. I consented because a result that arrives only when its author directs the sequence is a party trick, not knowledge. The Queen approached a dark triangle twice, avoided it once, and ignored the rest. The pattern did not survive the afternoon. Mathilde was disappointed. I was furious, but chiefly with the cards, which had been cut from inferior stock and bent in the damp. Lenz had prepared a second batch. We repeated the sequence on another day with no improvement. I recorded the failure and refused Mathilde's suggestion that we name the Queen's favorite shape. If I must bestow titles upon insignificant things, there are members of the faculty still available.

candidates.title: An Honest Catalogue of Imperfections
candidates.source_excerpt: I wished to prepare a catalogue of the little court suitable for a visitor who had offered to purchase drawings. The Queen's profile deserved first place, followed by the Ballerina and the King. Anna placed her own list beside mine. Her headings were not beauty, proportion, and dignity but movement, tolerance of cold, appetite, and response to unfamiliar objects. The Devil, whom I had assigned an uncertain rank, led in two practical categories. I accused Anna of preparing an inventory of kitchen servants. She accused me of preparing a catalogue of porcelain. We retained both. A visiting collector favored my list and pronounced himself delighted. I found myself examining Anna's afterward. It had the intolerable merit of explaining why several apparently ungainly subjects survived difficulties that defeated their more finished companions.

candidates.title: The Refusal I Had Prepared
candidates.source_excerpt: Adler asked permission to describe one of my miniature figures in an exhibition catalogue. I had prepared a refusal involving the word desecration, which I was certain he would find memorable. Mathilde read his proposed description first. It was concise, accurate, and gave the creature no name. I objected that to omit the Queen's title was to strip her of individuality. Julian asked whether the title belonged to her or to me. That question had become a tiresome favorite among my friends, as though good questions improved with repeated use. I offered to supply a revised caption. He accepted, provided its claims remained observational. We spent two afternoons disputing eight lines. The final description mentioned my authorship, her voluntary choices, and the limits of what the display could prove. It was better than either of our drafts. The exhibition proceeded without the living Queen, using a drawing instead. I told everyone that I had refused a vulgar public spectacle. I did not mention that Adler had suggested the drawing before I did.
