candidates.title: A Small Funeral for a Name
candidates.source_excerpt: A man named Bernhard Vogel was buried on a morning so windy the priest's pages would not remain in order. I had never met him. He had copied some of my observations for a private catalogue and once sent a correction with the modest request that his name not be printed. Marta Voss remarked that he might have wished to protect his employment. Georg knew the family and said Vogel had disliked crowds in life. I went because his correction had saved me from an error in a botanical comparison, and because I thought attendance might be the only acknowledgement left available. There were eleven mourners, counting me. No one recognized my connection to the deceased, which initially offended me and then seemed appropriate. After the service I placed the corrected page inside my coat rather than leaving it on the grave. Voss asked what I had said to his widow. Nothing, I replied. She had enough people telling her what sort of man her husband had been. I thought it sufficient to have come. I could not persuade Voss that I meant this modestly.

candidates.title: The Inn's Second Guest
candidates.source_excerpt: We stopped at an inn whose landlord mistook Voss for my daughter and quoted a single room. She corrected the relationship without looking at me. I was tempted to improve his education in several directions, but she had already secured two rooms and a place for our specimens beside the cold cellar wall. At supper a stranger asked whether our crates contained explosives. I told him they contained something more offensive to the complacent. Voss said they were plants. He lost interest. In the morning one crate had been moved to make way for the inn's apples. Our records showed no damage, yet Voss insisted upon recording the interruption. I admired her exactitude and resented how effectively a simple answer had protected our work. We travelled on in silence until she produced a pear stolen, she said, from the breakfast tray. I ate half and said nothing of theft.

candidates.title: The Margin Which Voss Would Not Close
candidates.source_excerpt: Voss found the French article while checking whether a passage from my old paper had been quoted honestly in a newer German essay. She read the portion concerning the obligations of a maker and asked why my reply had concerned the stupidity of regulations rather than the creature's possible sufferings. I began the familiar story of an ambitious journalist hunting scandal. She stopped me and asked which sentence Jolivet had invented. I could name none. I accused her of finding me too entertaining an enemy. She said that an interesting man and an adequate argument were separate objects. Then she returned to her botanical notes, leaving the newspaper open on the table. Later, while she measured a plant structure under poor light, I moved the lamp closer without speaking. Her thanks were casual. I remembered the reporter moving his chair to see my diagram and felt an old pang that was neither entirely anger nor desire. Perhaps being truly read is a form of intimacy to which I am unusually susceptible.

candidates.title: The Poorhouse Petition
candidates.source_excerpt: Reuter brought a request for a practical lecture at the poorhouse. The superintendent wished us to demonstrate new principles of circulation and had offered living residents as convenient examples. Henry was delighted by the prospect of cases not confined to anatomy books. Clara asked who had consented, and Reuter answered that the superintendent had signed the invitation. She placed it beside a patient's unpaid bill and inquired whether either scrap of paper was the patient's own hand. I began to object that we were discussing demonstration rather than injury. In the end I went to the poorhouse with a blackboard and no instruments. Henry was disappointed; the residents asked better questions than the superintendent. I did not abandon the conviction that knowledge often demands intrusion. At my next lecture I left the rear door unlatched. Two listeners went out during the introductory remarks. The others stayed and argued.

question: A conference committee credits Pretorius for measurements Clara corrected and records she maintained. Which response is supported by both memories?

candidates.title: The Two Glasses of Gin
candidates.source_excerpt: Leonie offered me gin after a meeting in which a committee member had suggested that my investigations would be more acceptable if I called them demonstrations of divine craftsmanship. She filled two small glasses, then took one away when I said I had never been drunk in my life. I protested that this was no reason to be parsimonious. Clara appeared to collect a packet of dressings and observed that men who advertised themselves as immune to a weakness were usually planning to indulge it. I lifted the remaining glass and declared that gin was my one concession to human frailty. They were not impressed. The liquor was coarse, and the lemon peel had been cut with a pair of costume shears. For all that, I remember the kitchen heat, the smell of starch, and the extraordinary relief of having no one ask me to defend a theory for nearly an hour. Thereafter I sometimes described gin as a weakness. It was considerably easier than naming the company.

candidates.title: A Number Removed
candidates.source_excerpt: Reuter found an arithmetic error in my summary of survival intervals, and a particularly cruel one, for it improved the apparent outcome precisely where the committee wished to see it. I could have corrected the working papers quietly, leaving the summary untouched. Instead I took a knife to the number and rewrote the page. Clara, waiting in the corridor, said that no one on the committee would have checked it. I replied that I might have. This was not a declaration of virtue. I was furious that an error of my own had provided the institution with an argument it did not deserve. The new figure made no difference to the verdict. I still remember the scraping of the knife and the clock that continued ticking while I debated whether a single honest number could cost a man his laboratory.

candidates.title: The News from the Windmill
candidates.source_excerpt: The second account came in June, and with it a confirmation from a correspondent not given to the more picturesque forms of falsehood. Henry Frankenstein had brought a being to life from dead flesh. The creature had survived the fire at a windmill. Henry was alive. I entered the claims, their sources, and the matters still concealed from me in the blue ledger. The diagram of separate organs lay open on the table, its corners curled with age. Henry had pursued assembly while I pursued growth, and there, at last, was a result no committee could dismiss by refusing to inspect it. Anna asked whether I would seek him. Voss asked what I would want when I found him. I closed the travelling case and looked through the east window toward the road. I offered neither woman an answer. The Queen moved upon her ledge behind me. I remained in the tower that night, with the old drawings spread beneath my hand.

candidates.title: The Tower with Three Dry Rooms
candidates.source_excerpt: The tower was cheaper than any respectable laboratory and possessed three rooms that remained dry in rain, a virtue sufficient to outweigh its missing stair rail. Lenz tested the upper floor with his boot and refused to carry a jar across it until the beams had been supported. I called his caution provincial. He asked whether I preferred the Queen to arrive on the ground floor by gravity. Clara brought straw, blankets and two pails whose contents were not to be confused. We moved the creatures before the books, the books before my clothes. At dusk the Queen was settled in the least draughty corner, and I discovered that my own bed was damp. I slept beside the heating stove and congratulated myself on having chosen independence.

candidates.title: The Coat at the Station
candidates.source_excerpt: Vienna greeted me with sleet and the smell of coal. Adler had brought a second coat because mine, he said, was manifestly designed for a city in which the weather respected academic seniority. I refused it, then accepted it when a gust entered the station platform and settled that question experimentally. We spent the morning among display cases whose makers had improved their lenses and concealed the compromises in their mounts. At lunch Julian spoke of a brother with whom he had not corresponded for twelve years. He told the story without asking mine, a courtesy I found disconcerting. I said little. He did not treat silence as a challenge to be overcome. When we parted he asked only that the coat be returned by post. I sent it with a list of corrections to the exhibition catalogue and a note advising him to replace its missing cuff button. The button had been missing when he lent it. In the parcel I enclosed a new one, wrapped separately so it would not appear that I had repaired his garment out of sentiment.

candidates.title: The Blind Naming
candidates.source_excerpt: I claimed I could distinguish the promising vessels at a glance. Clara said this was the kind of claim made by men who never allowed anyone to rearrange a shelf. Lenz tied blue ribbons to the lids, marked the bottoms, and asked me to select the soundest specimens while the shutters stood half closed. I chose the most attractive three. Two had already failed. The plain vessel which I passed over continued its obscure growth for another month. I accused Lenz of allowing the light to mislead me. She opened the shutters and invited me to repeat the trial. I did better, though not well enough to justify the original boast. Lenz wrote the scores and showed no particular delight in defeating me. I found her lack of triumph peculiarly difficult to resent.

candidates.title: The Living Specimen and the Silk
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde came with a proof of my account of miniature differentiation. I had described a series of splendid appearances, each one supported by precise adjectives and very little troublesome arithmetic. She tapped the passage in which I called two vessels successful, then placed beside it the record showing that both had ceased to respond. I asked whether a printer was now to adjudicate viability. She said a reader would do so if I gave him the opportunity. We worked through a rainy evening replacing my most handsome sentences with measurements and the names of failures. When I saw the result in type it had lost something of my elegance. It had gained the inconvenient property of being a document I could consult without remembering which claims I had embellished. We kept a copy beside the ledger.

candidates.title: The Newspaper on the Committee's Table
candidates.source_excerpt: Heller came to examine matters which a philosopher should not have needed to explain under oath. The committee wanted records of apparatus, the supervision of assistants, and the safety of certain investigations whose nature had already inspired more rumour than fact. When I entered the waiting room the French clipping lay among the papers. I knew the page before I could read the type, for one corner had torn beside Jolivet's last paragraph. I asked whether an article by a journalist constituted a scientific accusation. Heller said that it did not, and moved it aside. The questions that followed concerned invoices, access to the workrooms, and decisions I had taken without adequate consultation. Several were fair. I answered all of them as though they were variations of the question about my soul. Afterward I recalled Heller's hand pushing the newspaper out of the centre of the table. At the time I took the gesture as proof that the proceedings were absurd. In truth, he had been showing me where the actual difficulty lay.

candidates.title: The Empty Control Vessel
candidates.source_excerpt: A preserved sample clouded its glass twice. Marta suspected the vessel rather than anything living. We placed an empty control beside it. The empty glass clouded as well. Our result withdrew an attractive answer without providing a replacement. The room smelled of old cork and damp wood. Clara traced the dampness to a leaking sill, which I had ignored because it made the northern light picturesque. We moved the rack and repeated the observations over several weeks. I was tempted to declare the control contaminated merely to regain my earlier theory. Instead I wrote unresolved across the page. Later visitors praised our photographs of clouded glass for their mysterious depth. I refrained from describing that effect as a discovery.

candidates.title: A Name Lost in the Lists
candidates.source_excerpt: Reuter asked me to inspect a series of records from men returning wounded after the war. One young assistant had been known to him by a nickname, yet the hospital's transfer lists had entered three different spellings of his name. The man's injury was visible; his subsequent whereabouts were not. I argued with the clerk over the mistaken initials until he permitted us to copy the surviving records. We located the assistant at another infirmary two days later. Reuter called it good fortune. I called it a victory over defective classification. The man himself was more interested in finding his spectacles than in our triumph. Clara supplied a pair from a drawer of abandoned possessions. I saw how an error in a ledger could turn an identifiable person into an administrative absence. The blue ledger acquired a separate index for those who handled or cared for my creatures. I did not call it sentimental.

candidates.title: A Cigar without an Audience
candidates.source_excerpt: The winter evening was quiet enough that I heard the ticking of the damaged metronome in the next room. I lit a cigar after supper and read a reply from Voss disputing my projected dimensions for a larger living form. The letter was severe, precise, and accompanied by measurements I could not readily evade. I put it down, walked twice around the room, and allowed the cigar to burn out between my fingers. I was annoyed with Voss for being absent when I had finally constructed a response. I began a letter, abandoned it, and reopened hers. Near the end she had added that she would be in Vienna until March and hoped I would not neglect the little creatures while defending an impossible machine. I wrote back with the corrected dimensions first. Then, beneath my signature, I asked whether she would require anything from Ingolstadt. I did not include an explanation for the question.

candidates.title: The Chair at the Back of the Hall
candidates.source_excerpt: I came to the municipal hall for a lecture on acoustics and found a woman in shirtsleeves striking the floor with the butt of a broom. Each blow summoned a dull complaint from beneath the boards. She was testing the platform before the evening's recital. I offered a more refined method of locating the loose joists, which she rejected because she had already found them. Her name was Leonie Rausch. She repaired costumes, altered scenery, and regarded scholars as men who expected someone else to fetch the ladder. I watched her wedge a scrap of wood beneath the offending plank, then clap at the rear wall to hear how the room returned the sound. When I asked whether she knew anything of Helmholtz, she asked whether Helmholtz had ever tried to make a tenor audible over an audience eating nuts. I went home irritated and borrowed a book on the physiology of hearing. The next week I returned with measurements. She had repaired the platform in the meantime. The book was not wasted, although my visit appeared to be.

candidates.title: A Request for Reconsideration
candidates.source_excerpt: The committee had heard its witnesses by June, though it had not yet pronounced sentence. I was allowed to submit a statement of reconsideration. Kappel brought me the official form, two pages of ruled paper, and advice to say that the observations were incomplete and the circumstances regrettable. I wrote that they were incomplete because life itself was not finished and that regret would not improve a measurement. Heller, who had come to collect another document, read the page with a tired expression. He said that I had once been capable of winning an argument without forcing an enemy to lose his dignity. I asked whether the committee had extended me that courtesy. He did not answer. I filed the statement. For many years I told the story as one of heroic refusal. Sometimes I remember the unused sheet Kappel had left beneath my hand, and that I might have written something else without falsifying a single fact.

candidates.title: The Acknowledgment Without a Demand
candidates.source_excerpt: Julian wrote to say that he had found the restorer he sought and intended to remain in Vienna for the year. Voss thought I might congratulate him. I composed a note offering advice upon the management of an instrument workshop, a subject on which I possessed opinions but no workshop. After reading it I tore it across the signature. My second letter contained three sentences: his search had produced a result, his catalogue description of the Queen remained useful, and I trusted he would find suitable work for his hands. That final remark was perilously personal. I sent it before I could replace it with a joke. The reply arrived a month later. He thanked me, said his left hand had improved somewhat, and enclosed a lens washer I had been unable to obtain locally. Nothing further was implied. I examined the washer for defects, found none, and put it to use. It was the most satisfactory correspondence we had exchanged in years, not least because neither party had been forced to explain himself.

candidates.title: The Corrected Diagram
candidates.source_excerpt: Henry returned the anatomical drawing I had lent him with a correction in red ink and a paragraph in which he carefully assured me that his alteration did not detract from the general argument. It did, of course, and I told him so. He looked miserable until I asked whether he had tested the new relation on another specimen. He had brought measurements in his pocket. I kept him until the caretaker called closing time and sent him away with three more drawings, each containing an error I had deliberately left in it. The following week he identified two and defended the third because the evidence supported my original version. I admired that defense. I also disliked the speed with which he was learning to dispute me. I had wanted a pupil who would exceed the syllabus. I had not reflected upon the inconvenience of his doing so in my presence.

candidates.title: A Journal Named for a Riddle
candidates.source_excerpt: In Munich a bookseller placed a new journal in my hands, its title taken from the creature that asks a question before it offers an answer. Sphinx was much too pleased with its own mystery for my taste, yet its pages included arguments about hypnotism and the soul which no professor of sound reputation would have admitted to reading. I bought the issue and a cheap notebook. Wernig asked whether I believed in spirits. I replied that belief was a lamentably economical substitute for research. In the train I marked claims supported by observations in blue, those supported by admiration for the claimant in red. The latter color soon dominated the page. I nevertheless ordered the next issue. An idea may be badly defended and still point toward a question worth asking.

candidates.title: The Man with Three Watches
candidates.source_excerpt: Faber's apprentice Pavel wore three watches, none of which agreed, because one had belonged to his brother and two had belonged to customers who never returned. The sentimental one kept the worst time. Pavel nonetheless reached for it whenever a whistle sounded in the street. Faber called that habit irrational. I replied that its purpose might have nothing to do with hours. The young man showed us that the back of the watch contained a scratched date. He would not explain it. I refrained from asking, which Faber regarded as an ominous novelty. Later Pavel designed a spring clip for one of my instruments and refused payment in cash, asking instead for a letter attesting to his work. I supplied the letter. Its praise was exact, its grammar impeccable, and its final sentence copied from none of my former recommendations.

candidates.title: The Invitation I Kept
candidates.source_excerpt: After the late summer when I had finally allowed the tower door to remain open to visitors, invitations became a nuisance of surprising frequency. Lenz asked me to a family supper; Clara enclosed a note that no specimens would be discussed at the table. I wrote a refusal based on a perfectly real series of observations. Before sending it I found an old invitation from five years earlier among the bills, its corners worn by repeated handling. The experiment was not time-sensitive. I attended the supper with a bottle of gin I considered a respectable offering and discovered that Lenz's daughter had become quite opinionated about my manners. She asked why I always arrived wearing a coat suitable for an execution. I told her it improved the appearance of a happy gathering by contrast. She laughed. On returning to the tower I filed the invitation with correspondence rather than accounts. I laid the invitation among Kappel's letters, though it contained no argument or observation at all.

candidates.title: A Sermon Without My Name
candidates.source_excerpt: Matthias invited me to a lecture on charity delivered by a visiting prelate. I attended because I was assured no collection would be taken, which proved untrue. The speaker denounced people who pursued knowledge without regard for suffering. He had never heard of me, yet several listeners turned their heads in my direction, which suggested the local imagination required little prompting. I rose to ask how much suffering the institution had prevented by refusing inquiry into its causes. The prelate replied with an account of his hospital work, naming patients and expenses in embarrassing detail. I was prepared for piety, not figures. Afterward Georg said I had asked a fair question and received a fair answer. Matthias said an opponent need not be imaginary merely because one preferred him that way. I contributed money to the hospital fund and gave my name as a misspelling of Pretorius so no one would infer a conversion. The receipt arrived under the wrong spelling and I kept it. I cannot say why.

candidates.title: The Little Examination
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde brought six blank cards, each bearing a different shape, and requested permission to hold them near the Queen's chamber in an order unknown to me. I consented because a result that arrives only when its author directs the sequence is a party trick, not knowledge. The Queen approached a dark triangle twice, avoided it once, and ignored the rest. The pattern did not survive the afternoon. Mathilde was disappointed. I was furious, but chiefly with the cards, which had been cut from inferior stock and bent in the damp. Lenz had prepared a second batch. We repeated the sequence on another day with no improvement. I recorded the failure and refused Mathilde's suggestion that we name the Queen's favorite shape. If I must bestow titles upon insignificant things, there are members of the faculty still available.

candidates.title: The Botanist with Ink on Her Sleeve
candidates.source_excerpt: Marta Voss had catalogued a botanical collection dismissed as too difficult for a woman by three gentlemen who could not identify half its specimens. I met her over a disputed entry. She showed me a dormant preparation recovered after a longer interval than I would have predicted, then produced the measurements before I could accuse her of relying on anecdote. Better still, she had read an unsigned paper of mine and found a fault in its conclusion without insulting its observations. At luncheon I asked for her address. She required, as a condition of correspondence, that I cease using the word 'provincial' to mean 'contrary to Pretorius.' I accepted no such constitutional amendment, but posted her a packet within the fortnight. She answered it, and in ink dark enough to be a challenge.

candidates.title: The First Coherent Response
candidates.source_excerpt: I shall not describe the preparation of the seed. The formula is not relevant to the recollection and I have no intention of donating it to posterity. What matters is that one minute developing form turned toward an intermittent shadow and continued to orient itself after the shadow was removed. Lenz suggested a mechanical response to heat. Clara changed the light and asked us to try again. We did. The little form did not behave like the first series of samples. I remained at the bench until my knees trembled, then went out to buy more candles. The grocer asked whether I had been drinking. I had not, which made the question particularly irritating. I wrote 'possible organized response' in the blue ledger and underlined 'possible.'

question: A specimen seems responsive but its welfare is uncertain. A public committee requests a demonstration that may impose avoidable distress. What response is better supported by both records?

candidates.title: The Drawing Returned
candidates.source_excerpt: Theodor received an offer to prepare architectural drawings in another city. I met him at Leonie's workroom, where half-completed costumes hung like people unwilling to commit themselves to a profession. He showed me the terms of employment. They were good, although not so good that I could not find objections. He asked whether I wished him to decline. The room contained an empty chair and a bowl of pins. I considered telling him that the laboratory would soon produce results worth witnessing. Instead I explained that advancement ought not to be sacrificed to an arrangement whose terms neither of us had properly established. He repeated the word arrangement as though testing a badly made hinge. He returned my lens wrapped in the theatre drawing on which we had first disagreed. I congratulated him on his future and left before Leonie could introduce sympathy into the discussion. Three months later I discovered that I had been consulting his notes on perspective while marking an anatomical proof. His absence had become useful to me as an excuse for a number of errors which were wholly mine.

candidates.title: A Number Removed
candidates.source_excerpt: Reuter found an arithmetic error in my summary of survival intervals, and a particularly cruel one, for it improved the apparent outcome precisely where the committee wished to see it. I could have corrected the working papers quietly, leaving the summary untouched. Instead I took a knife to the number and rewrote the page. Clara, waiting in the corridor, said that no one on the committee would have checked it. I replied that I might have. This was not a declaration of virtue. I was furious that an error of my own had provided the institution with an argument it did not deserve. The new figure made no difference to the verdict. I still remember the scraping of the knife and the clock that continued ticking while I debated whether a single honest number could cost a man his laboratory.

candidates.title: An Honest Catalogue of Imperfections
candidates.source_excerpt: I wished to prepare a catalogue of the little court suitable for a visitor who had offered to purchase drawings. The Queen's profile deserved first place, followed by the Ballerina and the King. Anna placed her own list beside mine. Her headings were not beauty, proportion, and dignity but movement, tolerance of cold, appetite, and response to unfamiliar objects. The Devil, whom I had assigned an uncertain rank, led in two practical categories. I accused Anna of preparing an inventory of kitchen servants. She accused me of preparing a catalogue of porcelain. We retained both. A visiting collector favored my list and pronounced himself delighted. I found myself examining Anna's afterward. It had the intolerable merit of explaining why several apparently ungainly subjects survived difficulties that defeated their more finished companions.

candidates.title: Science and the Petition
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde showed me a notice of the campaign associated with Magnus Hirschfeld and the new Scientific-Humanitarian Committee. Reiss, writing from abroad, had enclosed a few observations about the circulation of Ulrichs's work. I recognized the ambition to place scientific evidence against a penal statute, although I disliked the confidence with which some writers believed a sufficiently neat explanation of desire would compel humane conduct. Scientists could supply facts; lawmakers might still choose to be cruel. Mathilde asked whether I would sign a petition. I said that I would first examine its wording, which was true. I then neglected the matter for several weeks, which was another truth and less dignified. When I finally sent my name, I did so through her, with a note correcting two technical statements in the accompanying appeal. She told me that signatures had been requested rather than a journal referee's report. I replied that both deserved scrutiny. I kept Reiss's letter with the copy of the statute from 1871, two papers sharing a drawer despite an interval of twenty-six years.

candidates.title: The Demonstration Declined
candidates.source_excerpt: Heller offered me a public lecture provided I supplied a result and not another elegant conjecture. Henry wished to show our most responsive samples. I refused. They had responded on three occasions in four different ways, and a crowded room would invite us to call the most flattering outcome the true one. I lectured instead on vitalism, to twenty-six spectators who diminished to fifteen before the lamps were extinguished. Henry looked as though we had been sentenced. I had hoped for thunderous applause and had the decency to be vexed by its absence. Heller said an honest dullness was preferable to a splendid falsehood. I replied that he had made a profession of proving it. This was unjust, and he laughed, which made it worse.

candidates.title: A Place beside the Window
candidates.source_excerpt: Following my appointment, I bought a respectable writing table and transferred the specimens from the window shelf to a locked cupboard. Theodor came to see the changes and stood looking at the clear space where his portfolio had formerly rested. He congratulated me on the appointment without enthusiasm. I told him that faculty rooms required arrangement and that the drawings would be safer elsewhere. He said he had not asked whether they were safe. I answered with an account of the risks attached to loose papers and spilled reagents. We ate cold meat while the new table occupied half the room between us. Before leaving he set a wooden ruler beside the window, precisely where it had always lain. A week later I moved it to a drawer to make room for an anatomical plate. The ruler remained there through the entire winter, although I used inferior instruments rather than fetch it. Had I been asked at the time, I should have insisted the matter concerned only furniture.

candidates.title: The Room in Vienna
candidates.source_excerpt: In Vienna, Voss secured us entry to a laboratory where my name would have closed the door. She introduced me as a private investigator, which was quite true and wounded my pride only slightly. The director showed us preserved cultures whose apparent activity depended upon the hour at which they were examined. We spent two days quarreling over development and persistence. Rainwater came through the lodging-house ceiling and erased the tables I had spread across my desk. Voss produced a pocket copy. I told her she had the instincts of a clerk, and she replied that they were especially useful in the company of philosophers. We reconstructed the figures over disagreeable coffee. I bought her a better notebook afterward, without presenting it as tribute. She returned it filled with objections and two unusually useful diagrams.

candidates.title: The Little Imperfect Library
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde arranged the notebooks on the upper shelf while I dictated what I believed to be a definitive taxonomy of successful experiments. She stopped me at the first category and asked where the books on things which had not succeeded should go. Into the lower cabinet, I said, where they would not encourage visitors. She opened one and found the correction to the smudged calculation that had wasted our winter. We spent the afternoon sorting errors by optical distortion, instrument failure, mistaken response and unfortunate enthusiasm. The titles were appalling. The usefulness was undeniable. I retained my own index of achievements near the desk and gave Mathilde her unlovely library. There are mornings when I consult it before looking at my handsome work. I do not find this an improvement in my temperament.

candidates.title: An Invoice for Mercy
candidates.source_excerpt: A patron asked to see a figure whose appearance I had described as nearly complete. It possessed an irregular shoulder which no careful lighting would disguise, but its responses remained remarkable. The patron offered to pay for its replacement if I would discard it and show him a prettier version. I informed him that I was not a manufacturer of dolls. After he departed Clara brought me the bill for a sounder vessel, a sum I could ill afford. I paid it by sacrificing a fine wool coat to the second-hand dealer. I was not acting from tenderness, I assured her. The cost of producing a responsive being was simply too great to throw away on account of a shoulder. She asked whether I would give the same answer if the figure were hideous. I told her to bring the invoice rather than philosophy.

candidates.title: A Disputed Frog
candidates.source_excerpt: Emil Reuter said a twitch proved an animal had obeyed the experimenter. Heller had asked us to distinguish response from recovery; Emil preferred a demonstration that drew applause. I had watched the frog's leg move even when the stimulus was applied by a boy whose hands were shaking. The animal, I remarked, was not consulting anyone's intentions. Emil laughed, and I laughed too, though at rather different things. Afterward I found him behind the lecture hall replacing the soiled bandage on his thumb. He had been burned preparing the apparatus and had concealed it to avoid losing his place. I helped tie the clean cloth. The next week he lent me his German translation of a French physiology paper, still stained at the corner with iodine.

candidates.title: A Death with an Address
candidates.source_excerpt: Kappel died in June, having devoted the last of his strength to arranging books rather than composing farewells. His nephew delivered my old papers in a bundle tied with green tape. Inside lay the brass key I had surrendered years before, polished by handling and utterly useless to the lock it once opened. At the funeral someone introduced me as an acquaintance. I nearly corrected him with a list of the man's services to my work, then found the catalogue inadequate and held my tongue. Back at the tower I opened Kappel's last note. It concerned the copying of pages whose ink had begun to fade. Voss helped me sort them by candlelight. I set a second cup beside the ledger before remembering that the man who had always complained about my tea would not be arriving.

candidates.title: The Friend at the End of the Table
candidates.source_excerpt: Clara and Voss arranged Kappel's papers in the east chamber. They had divided his correspondence into subjects, dates, and matters which could not be reconciled by either. I objected to the third category as slovenly. Voss presented a letter in which Kappel described me as exacting but generous with time I did not think belonged to anyone else. Clara laughed at the accuracy of it. I demanded to know why he had not told me this while alive. She said he had tried repeatedly. We read no more of his personal observations that afternoon. Instead I asked to see his old catalogue, the one with corrections made in three shades of ink. I could recognize the years of his hand by the pressure of his pen. The two women left the third category in place. I never again insisted it be emptied merely to satisfy my need for a clean classification.

candidates.title: The Case Opened at Last
candidates.source_excerpt: The travelling case had sat beneath the east window for months, becoming such a fixture that Clara threatened to fill it with winter linen. I took the train to Munich and examined a collection of preserved plants, having entrusted the lamps to Lenz and the creatures' arrangements to Clara. I removed the old cracked metronome at the station when its weight offended me; a cherished error need not travel first class. Most of the collection was disappointing. One conservator, however, showed me how to record changes in illumination without disturbing a specimen. I copied his method and improved his chart on the journey home. The Queen had survived my absence without apparent distress. I called this proof that my arrangements were excellent. It was also a somewhat chilly welcome.

candidates.title: An Hour for a Sick Visitor
candidates.source_excerpt: Emil came up the path without his customary certainty and sat before I had offered a chair. He said the hill had been steeper than usual. When he tried to examine my tables, the page shook in his fingers. I accused him of having arrived ill merely to escape admitting an error, then brought water in a jug with a crack down its side. Clara found him an hour later, ordered the window opened, and treated my objections as an atmospheric nuisance. I gave Emil the guest bed and covered the specimen table in the adjoining room. Two days passed without the intended demonstration. On leaving, he thanked me for the bed but said nothing of our disagreement. I was offended by this selective memory. I have nevertheless kept a serviceable mattress in that room ever since.

candidates.title: The Broken Song
candidates.source_excerpt: A damaged tooth in the music box interrupted the Ballerina's familiar phrase. She moved at the usual interval, then stopped. I preferred to call this disappointment. Clara reminded me that she sometimes moved before any note sounded. We played the broken fragment by hand and obtained another interval. The metallic click of the failing mechanism troubled me more than the spoiled music because our previous results were no longer easy to compare. I had Lenz retain the faulty tooth when he repaired the box. Too often I had polished away the reasons a later measurement differed from its predecessor. The damaged part went into an envelope with its date. In time the click reminded me less of failure than of the relief of knowing which instrument had produced it.

candidates.title: The Address on the Funeral Notice
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde Rosen brought a proof of a funeral notice to Georg because a printer's compositor had omitted the street number. I corrected the punctuation before she had finished explaining why the omission mattered. Mathilde told me that the family had already lost one relative who had been unable to find the new house; a misplaced mourner was not a metaphor but a person. Georg took the notice and checked it against the parish records. I asked Mathilde why she tolerated work so dull. She said that the dead rarely complained and the living complained quite enough for both parties. We walked back to the printing shop through puddles containing fragments of election posters. I bought a packet of envelopes I did not require, then asked her to send future proofs of my scientific pamphlets directly to the tower. She asked whether that meant I trusted her corrections. I said it meant I distrusted everybody else's. She regarded this as an adequate contractual answer, if not an especially gracious one.

candidates.title: The Lecture That Returned in Print
candidates.source_excerpt: A pamphlet from another faculty reproduced an argument from my January lecture, including a mistaken spelling of a Latin term that had survived in the written notes. The author made no mention of me. Henry demanded that we accuse the man at once. Kappel advised a private inquiry; Heller suggested the error might have passed through students' notebooks without deliberate theft. I wrote a devastating letter and left it in my drawer. Then I prepared a corrected version of the argument and had copies deposited under my name. The unauthorized author published again two months later, this time with an awkward acknowledgment. I considered that partial justice. Henry asked why I had not sent the accusation. I replied that I had preferred an enduring record to a moment's revenge. I neglected to mention the evenings I had spent imagining the revenge in gratifying detail.

candidates.title: The Objection Worth Keeping
candidates.source_excerpt: A man introduced me at an informal gathering near the physicians' congress as though I had already enclosed immortality in a glass bottle. I corrected him, partly from conscience and partly because such a description rendered my achievement vulgar. I had no apparatus and claimed no official demonstration. The offprints supplied the evening's entire machinery. A French physician praised my observations on declining muscular response, then asked whether repeated stimulation had itself altered the preparation. For three minutes I disliked him. Afterward I wrote the objection into my notebook before the compliments, though I entered those also. Two other gentlemen wished to claim my work for opposite schools of metaphysics. Between them I felt almost rich enough to agree with both. When I returned to the hotel my cuff smelled of tobacco and my pocket contained three addresses. I had met scholars who thought me wrong without wishing me diminished. There was more pleasure in it than I had expected.

candidates.title: The First Coherent Response
candidates.source_excerpt: I shall not describe the preparation of the seed. The formula is not relevant to the recollection and I have no intention of donating it to posterity. What matters is that one minute developing form turned toward an intermittent shadow and continued to orient itself after the shadow was removed. Lenz suggested a mechanical response to heat. Clara changed the light and asked us to try again. We did. The little form did not behave like the first series of samples. I remained at the bench until my knees trembled, then went out to buy more candles. The grocer asked whether I had been drinking. I had not, which made the question particularly irritating. I wrote 'possible organized response' in the blue ledger and underlined 'possible.'

candidates.title: The Corrected Diagram
candidates.source_excerpt: Henry returned the anatomical drawing I had lent him with a correction in red ink and a paragraph in which he carefully assured me that his alteration did not detract from the general argument. It did, of course, and I told him so. He looked miserable until I asked whether he had tested the new relation on another specimen. He had brought measurements in his pocket. I kept him until the caretaker called closing time and sent him away with three more drawings, each containing an error I had deliberately left in it. The following week he identified two and defended the third because the evidence supported my original version. I admired that defense. I also disliked the speed with which he was learning to dispute me. I had wanted a pupil who would exceed the syllabus. I had not reflected upon the inconvenience of his doing so in my presence.

candidates.title: A Journal Named for a Riddle
candidates.source_excerpt: In Munich a bookseller placed a new journal in my hands, its title taken from the creature that asks a question before it offers an answer. Sphinx was much too pleased with its own mystery for my taste, yet its pages included arguments about hypnotism and the soul which no professor of sound reputation would have admitted to reading. I bought the issue and a cheap notebook. Wernig asked whether I believed in spirits. I replied that belief was a lamentably economical substitute for research. In the train I marked claims supported by observations in blue, those supported by admiration for the claimant in red. The latter color soon dominated the page. I nevertheless ordered the next issue. An idea may be badly defended and still point toward a question worth asking.

candidates.title: The Private Invitation
candidates.source_excerpt: Heller came privately rather than sending for me. He had heard descriptions of the miniature beings and wished to see evidence before the faculty was obliged to act upon rumor. Henry urged me to admit him. Clara said the conditions could be arranged if Heller agreed to observe without disturbing the vessels. I prepared three drafts of an invitation. Each seemed to surrender something to a man who might afterwards vote upon my work. In the end I showed Heller selected records and declined to open the inner room. He examined the curves and asked whether the living forms could choose not to be examined. I called this a moral question smuggled into a technical visit. He said technical questions frequently acquire occupants. We parted without an agreement. I still wonder whether a demonstration would have altered his conduct. That is not the same as wishing I had given him one.

candidates.title: An Unanswerable Question of the Queen
candidates.source_excerpt: The Queen began to grow still whenever we approached with certain instruments. Clara carrying fresh supplies produced no such effect. I called it anticipation. Voss asked whether odor, shape, or some regularity of our movements might suffice to explain it. We brought harmless objects to the bench and varied the observer, the order, and the light. The Queen was exquisitely uncooperative: responsive on one occasion, indifferent on another. I had made her, or at least had given the conditions in which she came to be; I had not instructed her to form expectations about me. If she had nevertheless acquired them, they might prove my deepest claim more decisively than any graceful limb. I was delighted by the thought and troubled by what those expectations might contain.

question: An unfamiliar organism shows coordinated movement once, and a visitor demands public certification that it is a conscious person. Which response best integrates the two archived observations?

candidates.title: The Photograph with an Empty Place
candidates.source_excerpt: Anna arranged to photograph the small instruments and their makers before several older pieces were dismantled for repair. I stood beside the workbench while she placed Lenz and Voss where the window light would reach their hands. I objected that the arrangement made me appear a visitor to my own laboratory. She asked whether I wished the instruments or my person documented. I replied that the one explained the other. She took two exposures and left an empty space in the first where Clara might have stood had she been able to come. When the prints arrived I preferred the less flattering one because Lenz's scarred hand was visible against the glass. I could not remember when I had begun thinking of that hand as part of the apparatus. Anna gave me the second print. I placed it in the ledger rather than hang it where visitors might ask for the names.

candidates.title: The Printed Marriage Notice
candidates.source_excerpt: I came to the shop for proofs and saw a marriage announcement in the newspaper stacked for wrapping. It concerned a man I had once known rather better than the world would have approved, now described in three lines as a respectable husband. A crushed carnation lay on the counter and marked the paper with a thin red stain. Mathilde pretended to be absorbed in an invoice. I cut out the notice with her paper knife, folded it twice, and put it into my pocket. She said nothing and brought the proofs. I corrected every comma with unusual severity. That evening I filed the clipping between measurements of vessel pressure where no rational archivist would think to look for it. It has no scientific value. I have retained things of less value under that pretext for much longer.

candidates.title: The Second Pendulum
candidates.source_excerpt: My new timepiece had behaved impeccably until I carried it from Faber's workshop to a lodging whose walls were wet with August heat. The needle drifted by a small but intolerable amount. I returned to Prague with the instrument wrapped in a towel and my indignation left altogether uncovered. Faber compared it with his shop regulator, then put both beneath a bell and waited. They disagreed in a different direction. He refused to call either perfect, to my profound irritation. I proposed that a reliable instrument ought to survive a change of climate. He replied that I was describing a saint and that his profession dealt chiefly in metal. I paid for a second timing device and carried away the two together. Their differences became a column in the blue ledger. It was cheaper than certainty, though not by very much.

candidates.title: The Performance I Cancelled
candidates.source_excerpt: A visitor requested a demonstration of the Devil's famous defiance. The flattering description nearly persuaded me. Anna asked whether I intended to repeat the saucer performance the creature had already refused. I prepared the gallery anyway. That morning I heard him tapping within the enclosure; he stopped when voices reached the door. I could not prove that the voices caused his silence. I could prove that no exhibition was owed. I cancelled it, citing unsuitable conditions, a phrase which rescued a portion of my dignity. The visitor replied that science had grown sentimental. I kept the letter because the accusation was almost handsome enough to borrow.

candidates.title: The Essay No One Read
candidates.source_excerpt: My essay defined the living organism by the continuance of its internal arrangement rather than by its resemblance to a familiar beast. Thirty-seven pages, which I considered a model of brevity. Heller returned it with the question: would a clock qualify? I had thought the distinction too obvious to require stating. He had therefore found the exact place to apply his knife. I spent two weeks in a clockmaker's shop, where a handsome mechanism expired whenever its spring ran down and never once repaired itself. My second paper concerned maintenance, repair, and the difference between borrowed motion and organized persistence. Heller wrote 'Closer' beneath the final paragraph. I kept that sheet. I cannot say what became of his more generous compliments to other men.

candidates.title: The First Coherent Response
candidates.source_excerpt: I shall not describe the preparation of the seed. The formula is not relevant to the recollection and I have no intention of donating it to posterity. What matters is that one minute developing form turned toward an intermittent shadow and continued to orient itself after the shadow was removed. Lenz suggested a mechanical response to heat. Clara changed the light and asked us to try again. We did. The little form did not behave like the first series of samples.
