candidates.title: The Borrowed Name
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde introduced me to Max Reiss, a schoolteacher who wished to have a short defense of a dismissed colleague printed without identifying the author. Reiss was careful with his verbs and almost reckless with the number of copies he proposed to circulate. I asked whether the colleague had broken the law. He said that he did not know, and that the allegation had preceded any examination. Mathilde declined to print a name without the man's consent. I proposed a general argument about accusations unsupported by evidence and spent three nights correcting it. Reiss thought the piece too cold to influence the public. Mathilde said that my colder language might keep the teacher employed. We printed fewer copies than Reiss wanted. Weeks later he reported that the school had quietly ceased asking questions. I claimed no victory; no public correction had appeared. What I retained was Mathilde's insistence that the person concerned should choose how much of himself the pamphlet spent.

candidates.title: An Honest Catalogue of Imperfections
candidates.source_excerpt: I wished to prepare a catalogue of the little court suitable for a visitor who had offered to purchase drawings. The Queen's profile deserved first place, followed by the Ballerina and the King. Anna placed her own list beside mine. Her headings were not beauty, proportion, and dignity but movement, tolerance of cold, appetite, and response to unfamiliar objects. The Devil, whom I had assigned an uncertain rank, led in two practical categories. I accused Anna of preparing an inventory of kitchen servants. She accused me of preparing a catalogue of porcelain. We retained both. A visiting collector favored my list and pronounced himself delighted. I found myself examining Anna's afterward. It had the intolerable merit of explaining why several apparently ungainly subjects survived difficulties that defeated their more finished companions.

candidates.title: The Question Beneath the Twitch
candidates.source_excerpt: The nerve moved when I applied the current and continued to move after the animal from which it came could no longer answer any question. A visitor called it the soul reluctant to depart. Reuter spoke of a lingering spark. Neither had looked at the wires. On my table lay a dish with a chipped rim, two damp corks, and a fork of brass blackened at the contact. The little lever scratched a more intelligible argument than the gentlemen. I asked Clara to read the thermometer at the glass, then wrote three words in my blue ledger: movement, relation, person. I made separate boxes around them. She wanted to know why I had arranged them in that order. I answered that a person was usually the last thing the physiologist knew and the first thing the theologian presumed. My wit was wasted on a woman trying to prevent the notebook becoming wet. When I later gave the boxes scholarly titles, I did not admit they began as a precaution against a puddle.

candidates.title: An Anniversary Not My Own
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde's dining room was full of paper flowers and an absurdly large cinnamon cake. I had brought a manuscript in a leather case, believing this to be the subject of her note. The gathering celebrated her mother's seventieth year. No one asked about my papers. I sat near the shutters, drank weak tea, and endured a child's account of a mechanical toy whose wheels would not remain attached. When the child asked my opinion, I examined the axle and suggested a repair. Mathilde took the case from beneath my chair and placed it by the door, where it remained all evening. I objected when I left, saying that she might at least have allowed me a glance at the proofs. She reminded me that she had invited a man, not a manuscript. I remember the cake rather well. I do not remember what I had intended to argue.

candidates.title: A Night of Melted Snow
candidates.source_excerpt: Snow slid from the tower roof and blocked the outer drain, sending water beneath the glass-room door. Clara arrived with towels; Anna arrived with a camera she had intended to use for an experiment and immediately put it aside. We carried every living vessel to the dry chamber. The Mermaid's jar was heavier than it looked, and I nearly dropped it when my foot slipped. Anna steadied my arm and told me to pay attention to the floor rather than the specimen. She was right. We lost several loose pages and a box of old labels but no creatures. The following week I insisted upon a new drainage channel. I paid for the work with money reserved for an optical experiment, and did not regret the exchange until the invoice arrived.

candidates.title: A Place Card in Munich
candidates.source_excerpt: They seated me beneath a portrait whose owner was distinguished chiefly by the expense of his frame. At the table sat two physicians, clergymen of different persuasions, an enthusiast for spiritual inquiry, and a woman who knew rather more about instruments than the men who had introduced her. The room smelled of candle smoke and rain-soaked wool. I was invited to explain the paper, and the questions came with gratifying speed. The woman asked whether an investigator who produced a living subject would thereby possess a claim upon it. I disliked 'possess' and made an elegant little joke about the vocabulary of solicitors. Several men laughed. She repeated the question without the objectionable word. I did not answer it any better. At the end of the evening a visitor offered an introduction in Paris during the gathering of physicians. I pocketed the place card bearing my name in a stranger's fine handwriting. It was a more precious souvenir than my arguments deserved.

candidates.title: The Defense of a Boundary
candidates.source_excerpt: At my defense, one examiner asked about dormant seeds; another about sleeping men. I preferred the first question, because a seed makes fewer demands upon a philosopher's conscience. Heller wanted an observation that would defeat my thesis, an extraordinarily ungenerous thing to demand of a candidate already obliged to defend it. I supplied one. Afterward Reuter shook my hand, looking so grave that I was briefly pleased to have inspired envy. His mother was in hospital. We walked there with my thesis under my arm, and I carried it all the way back because no one had the sense to offer me a shelf. The doctorate followed. I was scarcely beyond my student years and had earned the title I had been using in argument for some years. My pleasure was considerable, even if it was not wholly decorous.

candidates.title: The Empty Specimen Drawer
candidates.source_excerpt: On my third day at the university, I was given a drawer that smelled of camphor and contained nothing except a dead beetle pinned through its thorax. Herr Kappel, keeper of the cabinet, called it an accommodation. I called it a warning about academic generosity. He had lost the key to the better drawer, or claimed to have lost it, and made me sign twice for a cracked magnifying lens. I spent the afternoon arranging the beetle's wings under the glass, discovering that I could change the appearance of movement merely by altering the angle of the light. When Kappel returned, the drawer was cleaner than he had ever kept it. The following morning a second key appeared beside my ink bottle. He never admitted leaving it. I never thanked him in public.

candidates.title: Two Contrary Letters
candidates.source_excerpt: Two letters arrived at breakfast. One announced that my paper had proved the immortality of the soul; the other accused me of proving its extinction. I placed them on opposite sides of my plate while I ate an egg boiled to a consistency which might have served as a new mineral. Neither correspondent had read the conclusion carefully. I drafted replies with equal severity, then softened both, for even those who misunderstand a man may invite him to speak. A shorter notice disagreed with my account of reflexes and quoted the figures accurately. It was the best of the three responses. Clara asked whether I would allow a critic to inspect all my preparations. I said he might see those suitable for public inspection. She noticed the adjective. We quarrelled until the kettle boiled dry, then laughed without resolving anything. It was an excellent week. People had begun to disagree with me in distant rooms. I could almost hear the arguments crossing Europe.

candidates.title: The Old Automaton
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde arrived carrying Hoffmann's tale of the Sandman and a mechanical bird whose owner had tired of winding it. She regarded the doll Olympia as a rather transparent indictment of men who prefer agreeable women to attentive ones. Lenz opened the bird and showed us a spring worn almost smooth where the mechanism failed to catch. I proposed that a genuinely living creature must repair some portion of its own disturbance. Mathilde pointed out that people also required repairs from others; she tapped Lenz's old burn scar without asking permission. We set the bird upon the window ledge, and its beak moved three times before falling silent. The King meanwhile knocked upon his partition until the Archbishop turned away. I disliked how easily the company transferred its attention from a machine to my little court, but I was not foolish enough to demand an explanation from a bird.

candidates.title: An Answer to the Count
candidates.source_excerpt: Agnes Bell wrote after reading the English vampire novel whose diaries and telegrams Mathilde had praised. She asked whether the monster in that book frightened me. I answered that the villain's appetite was ordinary enough; what interested me was the carefully organized coalition assembled to oppose him. Each member possessed incomplete knowledge, and the case advanced only when they allowed their fragments to form an account none could produce alone. Agnes replied that my admiration for the hunters was a surprising development in a man celebrated for preferring his own company. I objected that collaboration was not democracy. Her next letter contained a single line asking how I distinguished the two when a collaborator disagreed. I spent a week preparing a rigorous answer and eventually sent two pages on governance of scientific work. She returned them with three precise questions and a note that she would be away for Christmas. I kept those questions open beside the blueprint of the larger laboratory. Even a badly written English adventure, it seemed, could furnish a troublesome model for the arrangement of minds.

candidates.title: The Restorer's Second Visit
candidates.source_excerpt: Julian Adler came to repair a delicate catch whose failure I had attributed to careless workmanship. He showed me the wear had begun on my side of the apparatus, where a misaligned weight dragged upon the fitting. I disputed the matter for nearly an hour. He did not rise to leave, nor flatter me by yielding. Instead he placed the removed part beneath the lamp and invited me to watch it catch at precisely the point I had insisted was sound. When he had finished, I found another instrument requiring inspection. Its fault was trifling. He saw that at once and repaired it anyway. I do not pretend this was an experiment in companionship. It was merely that his departure would have interrupted an argument in which I had not yet achieved a satisfactory conclusion. He came back the following month without an appointment.

candidates.title: The Unsent Recommendation
candidates.source_excerpt: Kappel offered to write a recommendation for a stipend that would pay the rent and spare me a second winter without proper heating. The form required a statement of character. He read aloud the phrase 'obedient to instruction' and waited for me to object. I obliged. For an hour we altered the sentence until it said I completed assigned work but disputed its assumptions. My father, asked to countersign my application, returned it with a note that the second clause would cost me the stipend. It did. Kappel retained the draft in his cabinet and found me other temporary access to the instruments. I declared the lost money insignificant. That evening I counted what remained in my purse twice. Pride has always been more agreeable when someone else supplies the coal; that fact has never persuaded me to surrender it.

candidates.title: The Queen and the Stranger
candidates.source_excerpt: The Queen began approaching Voss whenever she entered the room. She had once shown the same inclination toward Clara; I had assumed it would eventually extend to the person who had made and sustained her. Evidently monarchy possesses no instinct for gratitude. I changed the hours of Voss's visits, rotated the vessel, checked the light, and still the little ingrate moved toward the newcomer. Voss said I was treating her as a student selecting a favored professor. I said a professor at least provides the education. Clara laughed so heartily that I nearly dismissed them both. I recorded every approach thereafter, including those occasions when the Queen came to my side, a detail which I confess gave the table a more agreeable appearance.

candidates.title: A Bacillus at Breakfast
candidates.source_excerpt: Reuter laid a Berlin report beside the marmalade and spoke with uncommon animation of Koch's announcement concerning tuberculosis. The decisive thing, he said, was not the beauty of the organism but its demonstrable association with disease. I admired the discipline of the claim and objected to his pleasure in rendering a great mystery small enough to stain upon a slide. Voss observed that I had made my own living creatures small enough to stand in glass. There are occasions when a woman should be made to pay for her analogies. I purchased Reuter's breakfast instead. That afternoon he showed me a row of ordinary hospital notes whose exact dates mattered more than their eloquence. I had expected him to praise discovery. Instead he praised the clerks who made it possible to determine what had actually happened. I found the sentiment revoltingly sound.

question: A close companion asks for a direct answer about a long-promised day together, while another interesting laboratory task has arrived. Which response best addresses the relationship costs shown in both memories?

candidates.title: The Inn's Second Guest
candidates.source_excerpt: We stopped at an inn whose landlord mistook Voss for my daughter and quoted a single room. She corrected the relationship without looking at me. I was tempted to improve his education in several directions, but she had already secured two rooms and a place for our specimens beside the cold cellar wall. At supper a stranger asked whether our crates contained explosives. I told him they contained something more offensive to the complacent. Voss said they were plants. He lost interest. In the morning one crate had been moved to make way for the inn's apples. Our records showed no damage, yet Voss insisted upon recording the interruption. I admired her exactitude and resented how effectively a simple answer had protected our work. We travelled on in silence until she produced a pear stolen, she said, from the breakfast tray. I ate half and said nothing of theft.

candidates.title: An Account Against the Wall
candidates.source_excerpt: Lenz arrived with an invoice and refused another promise of payment in the form of future scientific fame. My new laboratory required glass joints he could have sold to paying customers, and his marriage had not abolished the cost of coal. I said I had invested in his skill. He asked whether he might invest my admiration at the baker's. Clara, who had accompanied him, said nothing. I sold an engraved instrument I seldom used and paid two-thirds of the account. Lenz gave me a further month for the balance, but he no longer accepted orders without written terms. I called his policy officious. He continued supplying the finest vessels I could obtain. To this day I distrust a man who asks for blind faith in a partnership. I also resent being reminded that the distrust was taught to me by a glassblower.

candidates.title: The Botanist with Ink on Her Sleeve
candidates.source_excerpt: Marta Voss had catalogued a botanical collection dismissed as too difficult for a woman by three gentlemen who could not identify half its specimens. I met her over a disputed entry. She showed me a dormant preparation recovered after a longer interval than I would have predicted, then produced the measurements before I could accuse her of relying on anecdote. Better still, she had read an unsigned paper of mine and found a fault in its conclusion without insulting its observations. At luncheon I asked for her address. She required, as a condition of correspondence, that I cease using the word 'provincial' to mean 'contrary to Pretorius.' I accepted no such constitutional amendment, but posted her a packet within the fortnight. She answered it, and in ink dark enough to be a challenge.

candidates.title: The Tale Told at a Proper Table
candidates.source_excerpt: Mathilde served boiled fish and a plum preserve so sharp that it punished the tongue before one could admire it. Voss asked what had become of the handsome specimen I had displayed in a drawing. I offered an account of its promising proportions. She asked a second time. The fish cooled. I admitted it had not survived a modest alteration I had made in pursuit of further symmetry. No one expressed the horror I had prepared to rebuke. Mathilde asked how many attempts I had made afterward. The number was disagreeable. I gave it anyway, and conversation improved. Thereafter those two ladies developed the habit of asking for 'the other version' of any report I presented too elegantly. Their impertinence has preserved several useful facts, while rendering dinner a less restful institution than I had imagined.

candidates.title: The Devil's Reflection Refused
candidates.source_excerpt: The Devil refused his mirror one December evening. I had promised a demonstration to two friends, and the creature chose instead to sit with his back toward us, exhibiting a most unscientific talent for embarrassment. The King was unusually quiet, the Ballerina would not answer her music, and the chamber had grown cold. We restored the heat. The next day the Devil resumed his devotions before the glass. I wrote down every condition I could identify and refused to credit the warmth alone. Clara observed that I had been trying to summon yesterday's behavior from today's creature. An objection I had already entered in the ledger, though expressed by her with far less elegance. I changed my heading from 'obstinacy' to 'altered conditions.' I continued to call him the Devil. It suited us both.

candidates.title: A Journal Named for a Riddle
candidates.source_excerpt: In Munich a bookseller placed a new journal in my hands, its title taken from the creature that asks a question before it offers an answer. Sphinx was much too pleased with its own mystery for my taste, yet its pages included arguments about hypnotism and the soul which no professor of sound reputation would have admitted to reading. I bought the issue and a cheap notebook. Wernig asked whether I believed in spirits. I replied that belief was a lamentably economical substitute for research. In the train I marked claims supported by observations in blue, those supported by admiration for the claimant in red. The latter color soon dominated the page. I nevertheless ordered the next issue. An idea may be badly defended and still point toward a question worth asking.

candidates.title: An Ethical Error without a Violation
candidates.source_excerpt: Anna had prepared a flawless chamber for a trial intended to test how long a subject would tolerate an unpleasant change in light. The question had little value beyond satisfying my curiosity and proving that I could sustain control. Voss asked what I expected to learn that ordinary observation had not already shown. I began an impressive explanation and found it wanting halfway through. The little figure continued its daily movements while we argued. Finally I instructed Anna to return the chamber to storage. She asked whether she had made an error in its construction. Not at all, I told her. The apparatus was perfect. The question was vulgar. I resented having to distinguish between the two, and the distinction thereafter became one of my less advertised rules.

candidates.title: A Gift Refused for the Right Reason
candidates.source_excerpt: I presented Julian with an instrument restored so perfectly that even its former owner might have failed to recognize it. He admired the work and asked whether I expected him to take over the measurements I had been neglecting. I said I expected nothing. He opened the leather case and showed me the list of trials I had enclosed beneath the lid. Frost formed on his window while the lamp smoked. The silence that followed was one of those rare intervals during which my wit deserted me through no fault of the company. He closed the case and returned it. I carried the instrument home, furious with the ingratitude of a man who had apparently understood my intention too well. We exchanged ordinary letters afterward, without a ceremonial reconciliation. I still possess the unused instrument. Its workmanship remains flawless, a fact not entirely to its credit.

candidates.title: A Card Sent Back
candidates.source_excerpt: Faber forwarded a note from Pavel announcing that he would leave Prague to establish a shop of his own. I drafted a reply congratulating him while recommending that he postpone the venture until he had learned something of the world's hostility to independent craftsmen. Voss read the letter and returned it with a single word written in the margin: 'Yours.' I removed the warning and signed a shorter card stating that I would continue to purchase his work if the standards remained high. In December his first independent instrument arrived, packed in wedges devised by Lenz, with a bill neither discounted nor apologetic. It worked. I paid within the week. The card came back months later because Pavel had used my signature as a reference when securing his premises. I kept the returned envelope, amused that a modest courtesy had acquired commercial consequences beyond my supervision.

candidates.title: The Margin Too Narrow
candidates.source_excerpt: A colleague returned my preliminary argument with three pages of objection and a fold which passed directly through the diagram of a nerve. He disliked the phrase by which I had declared an animal remembered its last impression. He was correct: I had shown a changed response, not remembrance. I spent an evening inventing replies that would have embarrassed his ancestors, then substituted a less splendid sentence. When Heller saw the revised page he approved it without asking who had obliged me to improve it. I was annoyed that sound advice might pass for his own influence. At supper I quoted the correspondence so wickedly that Clara asked to see the parts I had omitted. I said she would find them dull. She insisted. I produced the letters and watched her read them in their proper order. Her judgement did not differ from his. It was a disagreeable evening for vanity and an exceptionally good one for the manuscript.

candidates.title: The Unbeautiful Survivor
candidates.source_excerpt: The ugliest thing in the cabinet endured. It was neither human nor even promisingly animal, merely an organized tangle which grew against the glass like a careless signature. Its symmetrical companions had failed long before winter. Clara moved it to the south window and covered the other empty jars with linen. I told her it was an insult to my method. She answered that it appeared to be having an exceptionally good life without consulting my opinion. One evening I caught myself making a drawing of the twisted root with uncommon care, following each detour of its outline. I did not make it beautiful. I made it exact, which gave a pleasure I had not expected. I still would not have shown it to an admirer of my miniature Queen. I was beginning to learn how many audiences I kept inside my own head.

candidates.title: The Hand That Would Not Settle
candidates.source_excerpt: Lenz's hands trembled slightly after a long day at the furnace, and I noticed it while he attempted a delicate repair. I asked whether he had been drinking. He showed me the blister beneath his thumb and suggested that I try holding the hot rod myself before diagnosing his habits. Clara bound the hand. We postponed the work. At the next visit I brought a padded grip devised from cork and cloth. It was a poor contrivance but useful enough that he kept it. He thanked me with a joke about my becoming an apprentice at last. I replied that necessity had forced the descent. I did not inquire whether the grip lessened his pain; I watched his fingers while he worked and could see that it did. In my notebooks I recorded the alteration to the instrument. I did not record the reason I had designed it.

candidates.title: The Coat with an Unfinished Hem
candidates.source_excerpt: I collected the last of my clothes from Leonie's workroom after the dismissal. My black coat hung from a nail with its hem still pinned. She said she had not finished the alteration because I had failed to arrive for the fitting on three occasions. I reminded her that my professional circumstances had become unusually complicated. She took out the pins, laid the coat upon the table, and said that a man who refused to stand still could hardly demand perfect tailoring. Clara arrived with clean linen for the tower. For a moment the two women discussed weather and mending as though my expulsion were a minor inconvenience to ordinary life. I found this intolerable. I paid Leonie in cash, although she had not asked, and left before either could offer condolences. At the tower that evening I discovered one pin remaining in the lining. I wore the coat for weeks with the point against my wrist rather than take it back. There is a difference between endurance and stupidity. On that occasion I probably crossed it.

candidates.title: The Agreement We Did Not Sign
candidates.source_excerpt: Julian proposed that we agree upon what our acquaintance meant. He was not asking for an oath, still less a public announcement, but he wished to know whether my arrivals and departures belonged to a shared arrangement or merely to my convenience. I reminded him that my research could not be suspended for the sake of domestic regularity. He said he had never asked it to be. I then accused him of expecting an affection that could be scheduled. This was an answer to a question he had not put. Finally he said that he wanted to be free to accept another companion without committing a breach of a promise I refused to name. The possibility annoyed me more than it had any right to do. I declared that he was entirely at liberty. I continued stirring my cold coffee after the sugar had dissolved. He said that freedom offered with visible resentment was still freedom, but hardly a generous gift. We parted with a handshake in the crowded room. I disliked his correctness most of all because it did not make him less desirable.

candidates.title: A Joke Received as an Answer
candidates.source_excerpt: Clara found me in the dispensary arguing with Reuter about the difference between an unsuccessful experiment and an incompetent experimenter. She asked whether either of us could distinguish the two before her midday customers arrived. I replied that the incompetent man usually spoke longest. Reuter laughed; Clara did not. A woman waiting with a prescription asked if we were discussing her physician. I could have made an explanation, but instead asked to see the prescribed dose and found it needlessly ambiguous. Clara corrected the label and served the woman. Only later did I discover she had kept my joke and repeated it to her apprentices when they began quarrelling instead of working. She did not credit me, nor did I ask her to. My amusement had done a small service which argument alone could not. There is no dignified scientific account of why I enjoyed that discovery.

candidates.title: The Unsigned Calculation
candidates.source_excerpt: Henry left a calculation among my papers showing an alternative relationship between the mass of a living preparation and the time required for its recovery. I found an error in the last line, corrected it, and used the amended figure in a private discussion with Heller. Henry overheard enough to believe I had adopted the result without naming him. He was correct. I told him that a student's idea becomes part of his teacher's work when the teacher makes it serviceable. He asked whether the same rule would apply when the student proved the teacher wrong. I had no satisfactory answer ready. That evening I added his initials to the page and left it where he would find it. He never thanked me, and I never repeated the performance. My admiration for his courage did not lessen my appetite for ownership. Both continued to grow.

candidates.title: The Man in the Black Cape
candidates.source_excerpt: I had not intended to cultivate anything resembling myself. Nonetheless the fourth figure emerged lean, dark and rather theatrical, with a black cape whose folds appeared before the rest of his costume had assumed proper definition. Lenz called him the Devil. Henry, shown the figure during one carefully supervised visit, regarded him with more unease than he had shown at the Queen. The Devil bowed toward his reflection in the glass and then turned his back upon us. I was delighted. Henry asked whether the miniature had learned vanity from its maker. I told him that resemblance proved kinship no more reliably than a portrait proved paternity. Yet I moved the little mirror out of the laboratory afterward. Certain jokes are more uncomfortable when they resemble observations.

candidates.title: Not a Patient
candidates.source_excerpt: A physician acquaintance asked whether I thought the attachments of men such as Reiss could be described as a nervous disorder. Reiss himself was absent. I refused the premise that his life could be converted into a case study merely because he was not there to interrupt us. Reuter asked, reasonably, whether my objections were scientific or personal. I said that a diagnosis required a defined pathological process, not an offended audience. He brought several contemporary works on the matter; I read them and found the authors capable of observing great detail while committing themselves prematurely to explanation. I did not therefore conclude that all men who desired men resembled one another, still less that each man must live by a single new label. That evening I attempted a study of the Queen's appetite and found her unusually indifferent to my arrangement. I recorded the result without inventing a syndrome of disobedience. I congratulate myself, perhaps extravagantly, on having learned at least one lesson about the difference between behavior and disease.

candidates.title: The Clockmaker's Dinner
candidates.source_excerpt: Novak had promised to inspect the travelling mechanism at the inn. He arrived late, limping, and spoke of his brother's long illness while the soup congealed between us. Voss listened. I checked the time twice and could not resist opening the instrument case. Novak closed it without raising his voice. We spent an hour discussing doctors, rail connections, and the indignity of standing in a corridor for news. Only then did he examine the gears. He worked in silence, his fingers black with oil, and corrected an error I had been concealing behind an elaborate adjustment. The following morning the mechanism kept time better than before. I have never established whether the improvement depended upon my patient listening. It is an experiment I shall not repeat deliberately. His brother recovered somewhat, which I learned from a postcard months later.

candidates.title: A Man Who Could Count
candidates.source_excerpt: Reuter ruined a week's work by confusing two bottles whose contents had settled to the same pale color. I expected a confession, perhaps a satisfying evening of reproach. Instead he made a list of everything we could still infer and put it beside the stove. The best conclusion was modest: we had no result. Heller read the list and praised Reuter's accuracy. I protested that accuracy without discovery was clerical virtue. Heller asked how much of the previous week's work I had privately hoped to count as a success before the bottles were checked. I answered with considerable dignity and a number I later reduced in the blue ledger. Reuter had the decency not to observe the revision. From that winter onward, I could be intolerable about method even when the method prevented me from being impressive. It was an expensive preference, but it was mine.

candidates.title: The King After the Fall
candidates.source_excerpt: The King had long since survived his fall, yet one stiff movement continued to offend me. I devised a support finer than a spider's bridge and placed it where his gait might be corrected. Reuter watched the little fellow avoid it twice, then saw a fresh mark where the support had caught his limb. He told me to remove it. I demanded a reason better than medical timidity. He showed me the mark and waited. I removed the support. Over the next weeks the King moved more freely, though never with precisely the grace I had intended. I considered this a temporary compromise. Reuter considered it evidence that the creature possessed a body and not merely a design. We were both correct. That did not make his silence during the procedure any less insulting.
